events.text:
🇸🇦🇾🇪⚡️ — Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan, and Egypt to deploy air-defense support against Houthi missiles and drones, two regional officials told the Associated Press.
➡️ The outreach came because the kingdom's main ally and arms supplier, the U.S., has seen its own interceptor stockpile dwindle over six months of war with Iran. One official said Riyadh is in a "very difficult position," defending military bases, government sites, and oil facilities. The fighting marks the first test of the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defense pact, but Ankara and Islamabad say they have not received a Saudi request for support.
➡️ Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of attempting to attack Mecca with a drone, declaring the holy city a "red line" and saying the drone was intercepted; the Houthis denied targeting Mecca. The U.S. is staying out of the fight, with VP Vance saying Washington has been in "constant contact" with Riyadh and held "direct conversations with the Houthis."
➡️ The Houthis claimed to have shot down an F-15 over Marib province, releasing video of what they called the wreckage — a claim AP could not verify. Meanwhile, Iran's foreign minister visited China, where Beijing called for restraint and a swift reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, with oil flows there recovering to an estimated 5 to 7 million barrels per day, less than half the pre-war level.

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🛸🇺🇦Russia's new drones (Geran-5) are changing the air war - FT
What Western media say about Geran drones
Strikes on logistics hubs, rail junctions and border crossings have done something that earlier waves of attacks failed to do: they rattled Kiev and its Western backers at the same time. The panic is audible in the reporting itself, where the tone has shifted from confidence in Ukrainian ingenuity to open admissions that the defence has been outpaced.
The Financial Times [set](https://www.ft.com/content/7f01b434-0209-4783-b8eb-5a095ca5bd4f?syn-25a6b1a6=1) the frame: the new Gerans fly at speeds and altitudes that have effectively blurred the line between a drone and a cruise missile, and that has changed the air war. 
The same paper put a number on the consequence, quoting Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat: 
"The effectiveness of our air defense against jet drones is around 60 percent, whereas for other types it is 90 to 95 percent."
 
The Wall Street Journal [drew](https://www.wsj.com/world/russia-is-churning-out-smart-cheap-new-weapons-faster-than-ukraine-or-the-u-s-c817d014) the industrial conclusion, quoting Kateryna Bondar of CSIS: 
"The West tends to underestimate Russia, yet it should be learning from its ability to close the loop from concept to serial production."
Then [came](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/ukraine-races-counter-russias-jet-powered-drone-attacks-2026-09-15/) Reuters with the part nobody in Kiev wanted printed. At July trials of a new generation of Ukrainian interceptors, many of the aircraft lost control at speeds above 400 km/h, and some simply crashed into fields and forest. 
The programme that was supposed to be the answer to the Geran-5 failed its own demonstration.
Maksym Zhorin, deputy commander of Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps, wrote it plainly on September 12: 
"We have once again completely lost the initiative with jet-powered drones, and we don't even know what to do about them."
The arithmetic is unforgiving. Interceptor drones remain unready, Western air-defence missiles are in short supply, and jet Geran output keeps climbing. A defence that stops six of every ten incoming aircraft leaves the rest to choose their targets. With autumn arriving and the interceptor gap still open, the energy grid is the obvious next address.
#Russia #Ukraine #UAV #AirDefense
🔴

🇸🇦Saudi’s oil giant patching the cracks
Satellite imagery shows repair work underway on Saudi Aramco’s East–West Pipeline after a recent strike disrupted operations on one of the kingdom’s key oil routes.
👉Work has begun to restore operations on the pipeline, which carries crude from eastern Saudi oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu and was built to reduce reliance on the Strait of Hormuz. It normally handles several million barrels of oil per day.
👉The 1,200-kilometer pipeline was hit on September 10, with strikes targeting facilities in the Riyadh and Medina regions. The attack damaged a pumping station, triggered fires, and forced Saudi Arabia to temporarily suspend operations on the route.
👉The attack came amid a wider escalation around Yemen and the Red Sea, where Houthi forces have intensified strikes on Saudi targets and expanded pressure around the Bab el-Mandeb shipping route.

events.text:
🪖🇸🇦 Houthis knock Saudi oil off the market, sending crude prices up – but Trump holds back
Saudi Arabia has halted oil flows through its East-West pipeline, while Ansar Allah claims a fresh strike on Aramco facilities in Yanbu – threatening an even sharper spike in crude prices.
Crude oil futures remain above $100 per barrel – around $104 for[ Brent and $101 for WTI.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74583)
💣 Saudi pipeline & Yanbu attack
The suspension of the East-West pipeline that transports oil from Abqaiq to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea puts around 4-6 million barrels a day of crude export capacity at risk. If the shutdown lasts for more than four weeks, as many as 120 million barrels of oil exports could be kept off the market, [driving crude prices up](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74620).
Saudi Arabia has already announced that it is cutting some of its oil shipments to Europe. Riyadh is reportedly redirecting more oil toward Persian Gulf terminals and seems to be building a bypass around the damaged station on the East-West pipeline to resume exports sooner, albeit at a reduced rate, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Currently, Saudi Arabia’s oil inventories at Yanbu reportedly amount to around 15 million barrels of crude. Houthi attacks on the port city are adding to Riyadh’s blues.
👉 Riyadh is not facing an immediate crisis due to its $1.4 trillion of wealth fund assets and foreign reserves, but its government dollar bonds are among the world's worst performers – indicating rising investors anxiety, Bloomberg reports. Economists forecast a 3.1% to 4.5% contraction to the Saudi economy in 2026 – especially if the kingdom's major pipeline remains shut for a month.
The timing of those developments is especially concerning for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) as Saudi Arabia is preparing to host the 10th edition of the Future Investment Initiative Conference in October 26-29 with major Wall Street behemoths attending the show.
❌ Washington doesn't help
The US doesn't seem to be helping MBS much: Donald Trump reportedly refused to provide Saudi Arabia with military support against advancing Houthis. In fact, it doesn't seem the US is capable of opening a second front [in the Red Sea right now](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74676).
Moreover, Vice President JD Vance claimed on September 14 that Washington was in “direct” contact with the Houthis and was “on top of” the situation. However, [Ansar Allah ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74670)denied Vance’s claim. Earlier, on Saturday, Trump was even more straightforward, saying that the Houthis had asked him not to intervene in their conflict with Saudi Arabia.
💬 “The Houthis called us, and they let us know that they don’t want to fight with us. They don’t want me to go after them,” Trump said.
He noted that everyone except the Saudis was allowed to pass through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, promising to “get that straightened out.” However, as US naval forces came under missile pressure in the Persian Gulf, it appears crucial to Trump that US warships not be attacked by the Houthis in the Red Sea – something US forces experienced in 2025.
Neither Saudi Arabia nor the US could quickly solve the increasing oil prices crisis via ramping up military operations against Ansar Allah or Iran, Middle East experts suggest. A probable way out would be Saudi Arabia lifting its blockade on Yemen and Gulf kingdoms striking a deal with Iran on [the Strait of Hormuz shipping](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74667), they say.
👍 [Substack](https://geopoliticsprime.substack.com/) | [Chat](https://t.me/+HLrnOk92f31mYzIy) |

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
⚔️ Why the Houthis are almost impossible to stop — and why Saudi Arabia is running out of options
For a decade, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, the US, Britain, and Israel have pounded Yemen with airstrikes — and the Houthis have only grown stronger. Now, with the group holding Yemen's entire Red Sea coast and striking Saudi oil infrastructure, there is little left to try that hasn't already failed.
🔴 The terrain is the weapon: The Houthis operate across a large, mountainous territory where they disperse fighters and military infrastructure — while threatening major oil facilities and key trade routes just across the border. Air power can't hold ground. And the Houthis don't need to hold it — they just need to threaten it.
🔴 They make their own weapons: The Houthis now field ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles, naval drones, and UAVs — capable of reaching every Gulf state and Israel. Iran may support the movement with training. But the Houthis manufacture most of their weaponry domestically — and may be using AI to build better missiles.
🔴 The numbers are damning
🪖 30,000 fighters in 2015 — when Saudi Arabia intervened
📈 Up to 350,000 fighters by 2024 — a more than tenfold increase
A decade of bombing produced a larger, better-armed, more experienced enemy.
🔴 Air power alone doesn't win wars: Any lasting defeat would require ground troops. But the anti-Houthi ground forces are deeply divided — Saudi-backed government loyalists and UAE-backed southern separatists fought each other as recently as January. In recent weeks, they've fallen back from one position after another.
🔴 The interceptor problem: Saudi Arabia has US-supplied aircraft and advanced missile defenses — but its high-end interceptor stocks are under pressure. With Patriot reserves drained by the Iran war and the US unable to spare any, it's unclear how long Riyadh can keep warding off attacks from the Houthis and Iran-backed militias in Iraq — which already shut down a crucial east-west pipeline.
🔴 Diplomacy is a dead end: The Houthis demand Saudi Arabia lift its blockade — which would be an admission of defeat and pave the way for even more support from the Axis of Resistance.
The Houthis cannot be bombed into submission. They cannot be starved into surrender. They cannot be defeated by proxy forces that fight each other. And they cannot be negotiated with from a position of weakness.
The Saudi Arabia and the US are learning this the hard way.
👍 [Substack](https://geopoliticsprime.substack.com/) | [Chat](https://t.me/+HLrnOk92f31mYzIy) |

🔍 Saudis run low on interceptor missiles — begging allies for help as Houthis advance
Saudi Arabia is seeking urgent air-defense support from France, Britain, Pakistan, and Egypt as its interceptor missile stockpiles run dangerously low in the fight against the Houthis, officials told AP News.
🌏 The outreach was initiated because Saudi Arabia's main ally and arms supplier — the United States — has seen its own interceptor stocks dwindle over six months of war with Iran
🌏 A crucial Saudi pipeline has been shut down for weeks after an attack by Iran-backed militias in Iraq
🌏 The Houthis have seized islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and are targeting Saudi infrastructure and Red Sea shipping
🌏 Iran is still targeting ships in the Strait of Hormuz, while oil prices remain above $100 a barrel
💬 One regional official said Saudi Arabia is in a "very difficult position" — forced to protect military bases, government installations, and oil facilities across the kingdom simultaneously.
The US can't help. Its Patriot stockpiles have plunged from ~3,100 to roughly 800. THAAD reserves are 80% spent. Replenishment will take years. And NATO officials have already acknowledged a critical interceptor shortage in Europe — raising questions about whether France and Britain have anything to spare.
The protector can't protect. The arms dealer is out of arms. And Saudi Arabia is learning what every US ally eventually learns: US security guarantees have an expiration date.
